narrative.text: Title block of the C2PA Technical Specification (Content Credentials). It states that the work is licensed under Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International, and carries an "as is" disclaimer: the parties disclaim all warranties, the implementer and user assume the entire risk of using the materials, and the parties are not liable for lost profits or indirect, special, incidental or consequential damages.
Heading that opens Section 1, Introduction; the block holds no text beyond the heading.

The overview motivates the specification. It says establishing the provenance of media is critical to trust, because mis-attributed and mis-contextualised content spreads quickly on social platforms and inauthentic content is rising, and because creators cannot currently attach metadata to their work in a secure, tamper-evident and standardised way across platforms. Provenance lets creators and editors disclose how an asset was created and changed; each change is added while the existing provenance is preserved. The C2PA developed the specification to enable global, opt-in adoption of digital provenance, informed by requirements from industry experts and partners including the Project Origin Alliance and the Content Authenticity Initiative, and notes that regulators could also use it to establish standards.

The scope: the specification describes the technical side of the C2PA architecture, a model for storing and accessing cryptographically verifiable information whose trustworthiness is assessed against a defined trust model, including how to create and process a C2PA Manifest and how digital signatures provide tamper-evidence and trust. It was written after the C2PA's Guiding Principles, which focus on privacy and personal control of data and on potential abuse; implementers are strongly encouraged to let creators and publishers control whether certain provenance data is included. Quoting those principles, it says C2PA specifications do not judge provenance data as good or bad, only whether its assertions validate as bound to the asset, well-formed and untampered. The specification should not harm content accessibility, and other C2PA documents cover user experience and threat and harms modelling.

The technical overview: C2PA information is a series of statements, called assertions, about matters such as asset creation, edit actions, capture device details and bindings to content; together they make up an asset's provenance and act as trust signals for a human. Assertions are wrapped with further information into a claim, which the claim generator signs on behalf of the signer with the signer's credential, producing the claim signature. A claim generator (hardware or software) binds the assertions, claim and claim signature into a verifiable unit, the C2PA Manifest (Figure 1), and the set of C2PA Manifests stored in the asset's Content Credential is its provenance data.

Trust in C2PA rests on the identity of the signer associated with the key used to sign a claim, per the specification's trust model. Combined with trusted time stamps, claim signatures can be validated indefinitely to determine whether a claim was signed while the signing credentials were valid and not revoked.

A worked example: a C2PA-enabled camera or phone takes a photograph and creates a manifest whose assertions include details about the camera, a thumbnail and cryptographic hashes binding the photograph to the manifest. The assertions are listed in a claim, which is digitally signed, and the whole C2PA Manifest (Figure 2) is embedded in the output JPEG, where it remains valid indefinitely. A manifest consumer such as a validator then validates the signature and its credential, checks each assertion, and presents the information and signature so the user can make an informed decision about the content's trustworthiness.

The design goals, listed in Table 1 so the technology works across hardware and software worldwide and is accessible to all: privacy (users control their information), responsibility (consumers can determine provenance), scalability (web-scale creation and validation), extensibility (others can add metadata and credentials without C2PA approval), interoperability, whole-workflow applicability (provenance kept from creation through publication), technology minimalism (rely on well-established techniques), security (trustworthy integrity and source, with expert review), content ubiquity (all common media types, including documents), flexible locality (online and offline), global universality, accessibility (e.g. WCAG), harms and misuse (avert harms, including to human rights and vulnerable groups), and evolving (continual review against these goals).

Reading guidance: the specification is easier to read in the parts relevant to one's role, in a useful order, than from start to finish. It lists three roles, each with its own section: claim generators (1.5), validators (1.6) and security reviewers (1.7).

A reading path for claim generators, whose core flow is to create assertions, reference them from a claim, include relevant ingredients, bind the claim to the asset, sign it, and package everything as a valid C2PA Manifest; examples are cameras, recorders, AI asset creators, editing software and transcoders. Required reading, each with its reason: the Technical Overview; selected Glossary terms; Assertions; Unique Identifiers (C2PA URNs); Binding to Content (hard bindings, and soft bindings such as watermarks for recovering a stripped manifest); Claims; URI References; Manifests; Embedding C2PA Manifests (only the supported formats); the standard assertions the generator emits; Cryptography; and parts of the Trust Model. Live Media is required only for live content, and Validation only for generators that support ingredients, since ingredients must be validated on ingestion — though any generator can use it as a QA checklist.

A reading path for validators, whose core flow is to locate the C2PA Manifest Store, identify the active manifest, validate the claim and signature, check signer trust and credential status, validate assertions, ingredients and the content binding, and return or display the results; examples are photo galleries, social media platforms, news publishers and verification tools. Required reading: the Technical Overview; selected Glossary terms; parts of Manifests; hard and soft bindings; hashing and signatures in Cryptography; parts of the Trust Model (validation states, trust lists, X.509 certificates); all of Validation, the core validator section; and the standard assertions the product handles. User Experience is needed only when results are shown to users, so as not to mislead them, and Live Media only for live content. Embedding, Assertions, Claims and URI References are listed as helpful context on the data structures.

A reading path for security reviewers, who check whether the trust model, cryptographic algorithms, validation process and security guidance meet current best practice. Required reading: the Design Goals (including what the specification is and is not meant to prove), the Technical Overview, Information Security Considerations (the core section, on threats, harms, misuse and abuse), the Trust Model, Cryptography and Validation. Helpful context: Assertions, Binding to Content (including the risks when assets are modified, stripped or matched by soft binding), Claims, Manifests (integrity, ambiguity, stripping and substitution risks), the relevant embedding formats, and the standard assertions relevant to the reviewer's threat model. User Experience is needed when reviewing user-facing trust signals, since misleading presentation can undermine security claims, and Live Media when reviewing live workflows.
Heading that opens Section 2, Glossary; the block holds no text beyond the heading.
Heading for Section 2.1, Introductory terms; the block holds no text beyond the heading.

Defines an actor as a human or non-human (hardware or software) participant in the C2PA ecosystem, such as a camera, image editing software, a cloud service or the person using them. A note adds that an organisation or group of actors may also count as an actor.

Defines the claim generator as the non-human (hardware or software) actor that generates the claim about an asset and the claim signature, leading to the asset's C2PA Manifest. A note says it is a component of a larger system, such as a library, SDK or shared service that a signer relies on, and is not the signer, so it does not take responsibility for the content of the claim or its assertions.
Defines the signer as the holder of the credential whose private key is used to sign the claim; the signer is identified by the subject of that credential.
Defines a manifest consumer as an actor that consumes an asset with an associated C2PA Manifest in order to obtain the provenance data from that manifest.
Defines a validator as a manifest consumer whose role is to perform the actions described in the specification's validation section.
Defines an action as an operation performed by an actor on an asset, with examples "create", "embed" and "apply filter".
Heading for Section 2.2, Assets and Content; the block holds no text beyond the heading.

Defines digital content as the part of an asset that is the actual content, such as an image's pixels, together with any technical metadata needed to understand it, such as a colour profile or encoding parameters.
Defines asset metadata as non-technical information about an asset and its digital content.

Defines an asset as a file or stream of data containing digital content, asset metadata and, optionally, a C2PA Manifest. A note extends "file" here to include cloud-native and dynamically generated data.
Defines a derived asset as one created from an existing asset by performing actions that modify its digital content, for example a shortened audio stream or a document with added pages.

Defines an asset rendition as a representation of an asset, either part of it or a wholly new asset, whose digital content has undergone a non-editorial transformation such as re-encoding or scaling; the example is a video re-encoded for a lower screen resolution or bandwidth.

Defines a composed asset as one built from a collection of parts or fragments of digital content, called ingredients, taken from one or more other assets. When it starts from an existing asset it is a special case of a derived asset, but it can also start from a blank slate. Examples are a video assembled from imported clips and audio segments, and an image with another image superimposed on it.

Defines an editorial transformation as one that alters the intent or the meaning (or both) of the digital content. A note says every editorial transformation is perceptible, but not every perceptible transformation is editorial.
Defines a perceptible transformation as one that alters how humans perceive the digital content under normal conditions.
Heading for Section 2.3, Core Aspects of C2PA; the block holds no text beyond the heading.
Defines an assertion as a data structure representing a statement about the asset, either made by the signer or simply gathered when the claim is generated; it is part of the C2PA Manifest.

Defines the assertion store as the logical collection of assertions that a claim references within a C2PA Manifest, stored together as one construct, and points to the Assertion Store section for its full structure.

Defines a claim as a digitally signed, tamper-evident data structure that references a set of assertions about an asset and the information needed to represent the content binding, and that declares any redacted assertions; it is part of the C2PA Manifest.
Defines the claim signature as the digital signature on the claim, made with the private key owned by a signer; it is part of the C2PA Manifest.

Defines a C2PA Manifest as the set of provenance information about an asset formed by one or more assertions (including content bindings), a single claim and a claim signature; it is part of a C2PA Manifest Store. A note says a manifest can reference other manifests.
Defines a C2PA Manifest Store as a collection of C2PA Manifests that can be embedded in an asset or kept external to it.

Defines Content Credential as the preferred non-technical term for a C2PA Manifest, so an asset's manifest store represents its Content Credentials. The term also names the C2PA technology as a whole and is treated as a plural noun: one manifest is a Content Credential, while several manifests or the broader concept are Content Credentials.
Defines the active manifest as the last manifest in a C2PA Manifest Store's list, the one whose content bindings can be validated, and points to the Manifest Store section for its full structure.
Defines provenance as the logical concept of understanding an asset's history and its interactions with actors and other assets, as represented by the provenance data.

Defines provenance data as the set of C2PA Manifests for an asset and, for a composed asset, for its ingredients, and points to the Manifests section for its full structure. A note says a manifest can reference other manifests.

An embedded HTML manifest store must be placed, Base64-encoded, in a script element of type application/c2pa in the document head, and validators must strip surrounding whitespace before decoding, with an example document shown.

A referenced HTML manifest store must be linked from the document head by a link element with rel="c2pa-manifest" and an href, which validators match on alone (type="application/c2pa" is recommended), and the external store must carry a content binding, with an example document shown.

A claim generator embedding a manifest store in HTML must include a c2pa.hash.data assertion, whose single exclusion range covers the whole script element when the manifest is embedded, and which has no exclusion range when the manifest is referenced by a link element. A note explains that the hash covers the stored bytes, so any re-serialisation of the HTML invalidates the binding by design, and advises embedding after final serialisation or using an external manifest.

Validators of text/html documents must parse the head as bytes for an application/c2pa script element or a c2pa-manifest link element, treat multiple matches as no manifest, and Base64-decode a script element's content. Resolving a link's external URI is optional, and any obtained manifest store is then validated through the normal validation process.
Heading that opens Section A.8, Embedding Manifests into Unstructured Text; the block holds no text beyond the heading.

Manifest stores may be embedded in unstructured Unicode text, such as text meant to be copied and pasted, as a sequence of non-rendering Unicode Variation Selectors, though this method should be used only when no other embedding is feasible and remains under review.

Unstructured text assets that embed a Content Credential must do so with Unicode variation selectors following the defined C2PATextManifestWrapper syntax and semantics, chosen because they are non-rendering yet valid Unicode.
Defines the C2PATextManifestWrapper as an optional container, encoded as Unicode Variation Selectors and present zero or one time, that holds a complete C2PA Manifest Store in JUMBF format.
Gives the binary syntax of C2PATextManifestWrapper: a 64-bit magic value "C2PATXT\0", an 8-bit version of 1, a 32-bit manifestLength, the JUMBF container bytes and optional trailing padding.

Explains the wrapper's fields: the fixed magic identifier, the version (currently 1), the big-endian manifestLength, the raw JUMBF manifest store bytes, and padding bytes that carry no meaning, must be ignored when decoding and allow a deterministic wrapper length.
Heading that opens Section A.8.3, Encoding and Decoding Algorithms; the block holds no text beyond the heading.
Each wrapper byte must be converted to a variation selector, with bytes 0 to 15 mapping to U+FE00 onward and bytes 16 to 255 mapping to U+E0100 onward, as shown in pseudocode.
Gives the pseudocode for decoding variation selectors back to bytes, inverting the two ranges U+FE00 to U+FE0F and U+E0100 to U+E01EF and returning INVALID for any other code point.

A non-normative table shows sample bytes with their variation-selector code points and UTF-8 encodings, and shows how the magic value C2PATXT\0 encodes to eight variation selectors that a validator decodes and compares to identify a candidate wrapper.
Heading that opens Section A.8.4, Placement and Detection Strategy; the block holds no text beyond the heading.

The wrapper must be a single contiguous, unsplit run of variation selectors immediately preceded by a U+FEFF marker, which counts as part of the wrapper for the c2pa.hash.data exclusion, and should be placed at the end of the visible text. A claim generator should embed at most one wrapper, and a validator finding more than one valid wrapper must treat the asset as having no manifests.

Validators must scan text for U+FEFF markers, treat the following run of variation selectors as a candidate, check that its first eight decoded bytes match the C2PATXT\0 magic, then parse the rest, ignoring any candidate that fails either step.

A note explains that a wrapper's UTF-8 length depends on how many bytes map to 3-byte versus 4-byte variation selectors, creating a circular dependency between the c2pa.hash.data exclusion length and the manifest bytes, which deterministic padding resolves by deriving the length from the manifest byte count alone.

Defines the deterministic target wrapper byte length for an M-byte manifest as 3 + (13 + M) * 4 + 6, covering the U+FEFF prefix, the 13-byte header, the worst case of 4 bytes per selector, and a margin of 6. Notes explain that the margin guarantees the gap to the actual length can always be expressed as a combination of 3s and 4s, aided by the low-range bytes always present in the header.

A claim generator should build the manifest store with a placeholder exclusion_length, compute the target length E, rebuild with exclusion_length set to E (repeating once if the CBOR integer width changes), and encode the wrapper. It then fills the gap between E and the actual length with a fixed number of 0x00 and 0x10 padding bytes, so that compliant generators produce byte-identical wrappers.
Heading that opens Section A.8.6, Validation Requirements; the block holds no text beyond the heading.

When validating c2pa.hash.data on unstructured text, the exclusions must match the wrapper's location, and the hash must be computed by removing the excluded bytes, normalising the rest to NFC and encoding as UTF-8, then must match the assertion's hash.
Producers and consumers must normalise text to Unicode NFC before hashing so that hash values are consistent across platforms.

The c2pa.hash.data exclusions use byte offsets into the stored UTF-8 text before NFC normalisation, and implementations must compute byte (not character) offsets against the stored text and ensure the exclusion covers the whole wrapper, including the U+FEFF marker and any padding.
Heading that opens Section A.9, Embedding Manifests into Structured Text; the block holds no text beyond the heading.

Structured text formats with comment syntax, such as source code, configuration files and markup, can carry a manifest store, either referenced or embedded, in a block delimited by fixed ASCII armour-style delimiters, which unlike the variation-selector method stays human-readable and needs no special Unicode support. Format-specific mechanisms should be preferred where available, and structured text inside a container format should have its manifest store embedded in the container.

The method applies to text/* files without their own embedding section, and to other plain-text formats with comment syntax, while HTML, SVG and TTML are excluded, and other XML formats may use XML comments. It must not be used for binary formats, formats lacking both comments and front matter such as CSV, or append-only files like logs and JSONL, which use the separate checkpoint method.

JSON-based formats lack comments and front matter, so they cannot use the structured text manifest block, but individual formats may define their own extension point, for example a root c2pa_credential member holding a manifest URI or a data: URI. The specification does not reserve c2pa_credential for all JSON, notes that strict schemas may reject it, and gives two example documents.

A manifest block must go inside an existing front matter section, or otherwise be a single comment line, a claim generator must not add front matter where none exists, and the block is delimited by -----BEGIN C2PA MANIFEST----- and -----END C2PA MANIFEST-----. At most one manifest block is allowed per file, and a validator finding more must treat the asset as having no manifests, while append-only checkpoint lines are handled separately.

In the single-line form the manifest block is one comment line with the host's comment prefix and suffix around the fixed delimiters and a manifest reference, which is preferably a URI or else a Base64 data: URI. The block is strongly recommended to sit at the start of the file but must go at the end when the first line is reserved (such as a shebang or XML declaration), sits after the header in formats like WebVTT, and should use preservation-hint comment conventions where available.

Formats with front matter, such as YAML or TOML front matter, place a multi-line manifest block inside it, with the BEGIN and END C2PA MANIFEST delimiters each on its own line and the manifest reference between them, the host's front matter delimiters not being part of the block.
Heading that opens Section A.9.4.3, Examples; the block holds no text beyond the heading.
A table shows single-line referenced manifest blocks using a sample manifest URL in the comment syntax of Python, JavaScript, SQL, CSS, Markdown, RSS/Atom and WebVTT.
Example of a single-line manifest block in a hash comment that embeds a truncated Base64 manifest store as a data: URI.
Example of a Markdown YAML front matter section containing a manifest block that references an external manifest URL.
Example of a Markdown YAML front matter section containing a manifest block that embeds a truncated Base64 manifest store as a data: URI.
Example of a WebVTT file with a referenced manifest block on a NOTE line between the WEBVTT header and the first cue.
For RSS 2.0 feeds the manifest block is an XML comment placed right after the XML declaration and before the rss root element, with an example feed shown.

For Atom feeds the manifest block is an XML comment placed right after the XML declaration and before the feed root element, with an example, and XML formats beginning with an XML declaration must place the block on the next line before the root element.
Heading that opens Section A.9.5, Hard Binding; the block holds no text beyond the heading.

A claim generator embedding a structured text manifest block must include a c2pa.hash.data assertion whose single exclusion range covers the whole block, reading files in binary mode, with start and length values defined for blocks at the beginning, at the end, elsewhere, or making up the whole file. Front matter delimiters are not excluded, line terminators must be LF or CRLF (bare CR files must be converted first), and the generator must not change line endings outside the block.
Points to the Validation clause for the normative procedure to locate and validate a structured text data hash.
Heading that opens Section A.10, Embedding manifests into WARC files; the block holds no text beyond the heading.

Defines how to embed a C2PA Manifest Store in WARC files (application/warc), the archive format of concatenated capture records, applying to WARC 1.1 and optionally WARC 1.0. Notes say this in-band provenance complements existing fixity practices and contrast its signing model with WACZ, PREMIS and BagIt.

The manifest store must be the block of a dedicated WARC record with WARC-Type c2pa-provenance, Content-Type application/c2pa, the manifest creation time and its length, without a WARC-Target-URI, and validators identify it by those two type values. That record must be the last in the file and the only one of its kind, and updates must remove it and append a replacement, leaving other records' bytes and hashes unchanged.

A WARC file must be hashed with a collection data hash covering every record except the manifest record, each hashed over its full uncompressed bytes including headers, and each entry's uri must be the record's WARC-Record-ID, which generators must check is unique. Continuation records are hashed individually and revisit records as they appear, without dereferencing.

The WARC manifest record may contain update manifests and compressed manifests, and an update is added by removing and re-appending the manifest record, leaving the existing collection data hash binding valid since update manifests carry no content binding. Because records are identified by WARC-Record-ID rather than offset, the manifest record's offset and length may change, and manifest compression is independent of WARC record compression.

Because record hashes are computed over uncompressed bytes, records may be stored uncompressed or recompressed under per-record gzip, whole-file gzip or WARC-zstd without invalidating the collection data hash.

When WARC files are concatenated or split, a claim generator must remove pre-existing manifest records and append a new one covering all remaining records, optionally citing the earlier manifests as ingredients, since any change to record content or the record set requires a new manifest store.
Points to the Validation clause for the normative procedures to locate the manifest store in WARC files and to validate their collection data hash.
Appendix B is a non-normative summary of the C2PA approach to user experience for provenance, deferring to the separate User Experience Recommendations document as the definitive guidance.
Provenance UX must be informed by the asset's context, and the recommendations, which are not mandates, describe interfaces for consumers, creators, publishers and verifiers across common contexts.

Lists four progressive disclosure levels for C2PA data, from an indication of presence and validation status, through a summary and a detailed provenance view, to a forensic tool showing signatures and trust signals; the block ends with a stray "== Information security" heading fragment, apparently from extraction.
